subject: Biology
topic: Robert Hooke and the discovery of cells
title: Robert Hooke and the Discovery of Cells
summary: The man who named the cell left no surviving portrait. Meet Robert Hooke, his book Micrographia, his lamp-lit microscope and his count of cork cells.

notes.title: 03 – Robert Hooke and the Discovery of Cells

keyPoints: **1665**: Robert Hooke published **Micrographia** and named the boxes in cork **cells** (Latin cella, a small room).
He designed his compound microscope and lit specimens with an **oil lamp** and a **water-filled glass globe**.
Cork cells are **dead**: he saw only the cell walls.
His estimate: about **1,259,712,000** cells in one cubic inch of cork.

sections.h: A famous scientist with no face

blocks.p: Robert Hooke (1635–1703) gave biology the word **cell**, yet no authentic portrait of him survives; pictures online are modern reconstructions. What survives is his 1665 book **Micrographia**, with huge engravings of what he saw through his microscope.

blocks.alt: Hooke's engraving of a flea from Micrographia
blocks.caption: Hooke's flea (Micrographia, 1665), printed as a fold-out as big as the page.

blocks.p: There were no electric bulbs, so Hooke placed a **glass globe filled with water** in front of an **oil lamp**. The globe acted like a lens and focused the light onto the specimen.

blocks.alt: Diagram: oil lamp, water-filled globe and specimen
blocks.caption: Lamp → water globe → bright spot on the specimen.

blocks.alt: Hooke's drawing of thin slices of cork
blocks.caption: Hooke's own drawing of cork.

blocks.p: In a very thin slice of cork Hooke saw tiny boxes arranged like a **honeycomb** and called them **cells**. Cork cells are **dead**, so he saw only empty cell walls, no nucleus or cytoplasm.
He counted about 60 cells in 1/18 of an inch, so 1,080 per inch.

blocks.alt: Steps from a line to a square to a cubic inch of cork cells
blocks.caption: About 126 crore cells in one cubic inch.

sections.h: Where Hooke fits in the story

blocks.caption: From cork (1665) to the cell theory (1838-1855).

blocks.p: Fun fact: this is the same Hooke as **Hooke's law** of springs, so one scientist matters in both physics and biology.

quiz.q: In 1665, Robert Hooke first saw cells in:
quiz.explain: Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw honeycomb-like boxes that he called cells.

quiz.q: The cells Hooke saw in cork were:
quiz.explain: Cork is dead tissue, so only the empty cell walls remained.

quiz.q: Hooke's 1665 book of microscope drawings is called:
quiz.explain: Micrographia (1665) included the flea, the louse and the cork observation.

quiz.q: Why did Hooke put a water-filled glass globe in front of his oil lamp?
options: To focus the light onto the specimen
quiz.explain: The globe acted like a lens, concentrating the lamp's light onto the specimen so it could be seen clearly.

simulation.reason: A history-of-science topic: the facts (dates, the cork observation, his count) are best carried by Hooke's own drawings, the timeline and the worked count. There is no variable a student can usefully manipulate.
